# Building for the future

## Authors

- Hugh Pelham<sup>1</sup> †

### Affiliations

1. MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology Cambridge United Kingdom hp@mrc-lmb.cam.ac.uk

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

As the staff of the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology settle into their new building in Cambridge, its director Hugh Pelham explains the challenges of living up to its prestigious past.

## Flexible working

The LMB is divided into four divisions—cell biology, neurobiology, protein and nucleic acid chemistry, and structural studies—and the heads of those divisions, together with the director, have the responsibility and power to make strategic choices. The passage of time has shown the wisdom of some of the choices made in the past. For example, when Greg Winter was being considered for tenure at the LMB in the mid-1980s, Fred Sanger, who was head of the protein and nucleic acid chemistry division at the time, suggested that he would fit into the division better if he applied his newly-developed protein engineering methods to antibodies rather than enzymes. Winter went on to humanize monoclonal antibodies, a breakthrough that has revolutionized medicine (and has also led to three highly successful biotech companies).

Sometimes, the strategy to follow is obvious because ambitious goals can take over twenty years, a great deal of persistence, to achieve. In addition to Winter's work on antibodies, other examples include the ongoing analysis of the nematode nervous system, and work on the structures of G-protein coupled receptors, which had its origins in early studies of bacteriorhodopsin. Again, history can be important: the LMB pioneered the use of both X-ray crystallography and electron microscopy to determine the structure of proteins, and we remain committed to being world-leading in the determination of large structures.

But the principle established early on was that the best way to make breakthroughs is to hire the brightest scientists possible and let them determine what to do. They are better placed than anyone to work out where the opportunities lie, and some of the greatest discoveries come from unexpected angles. Central funding and flexibility also mean that risk taking can be encouraged, and serendipity exploited.

In general, guided by the broader strategic goals of the MRC, we try to build on our strengths and to have groups with complementary but related interests. Nevertheless, when selecting new group leaders, we look for bright, flexible and imaginative scientists; these qualities are more important to us than the precise area in which they have most recently worked. Most of our recruitment is at the level of young scientists just starting a group, but more senior scientists are also attracted by the LMB ethos: for example, Venki Ramakrishnan, who shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009 for his work on the ribosome, moved from the US to the LMB because it offered the long-term support and relative security that he felt was needed to tackle a problem as ambitious as determining the structure of the ribosome.

In such an environment, the greatest pressure to do excellent, relevant and important work comes from one's peers. We encourage as much interaction as possible, and a conversation over coffee or feedback from an internal seminar can be as powerful an influence as any instruction from on high. Certainly as a young group leader myself, my greatest ambition was to be taken seriously by the intimidating intellectuals around the lab, who were very accessible and took an alarmingly close interest in what I was doing.

Though self-motivation is the rule, it can of course be steered both by explicit encouragement and by more subtle influences. It is no coincidence that the LMB is located next to Addenbrookes Hospital, or that it has contacts with industry. Indeed, we are building a closer relationship with Cambridge University School of Clinical Medicine by housing part of the Department of Medicine within our new building, and we have also space set aside for temporary translational projects and collaborations. Our experience is that the most successful collaborations arise though the active encouragement of willing partners, rather than any compulsion.

## Inside the new LMB

In designing the new building, we sought to retain and enhance the most important features of the old LMB, including workshop facilities and a rooftop restaurant, while increasing the space available for specialist equipment and making it easier to maintain and remodel the building without disrupting the researchers working in it.

We started with the benches and worked outwards—which was undoubtedly the best way to ensure that the building serves the needs of the scientists. To fit the LMB's hands-on style, there are write-up spaces close to the benches, and offices of group leaders are intermingled with the write-up spaces (Figure 2). The labs are partially divided, making it easy to move between them, to share equipment and to have groups that fluctuate in size. Equipment rooms are across a corridor from the labs and benches, making them accessible to all and creating a space for people to bump into each other: indeed, we took a conscious decision to make the density of scientists on each corridor the same as that in the first LMB building.

![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/00856/elife-00856-fig2-v1.jpg)

**Figure 2.:** A corridor in the new LMB building, with labs on the right and write-up spaces and offices on the left. The building is designed to encourage interactions between researchers in the corridors and elsewhere; such interactions were a defining characteristic of the original LMB building.

We also wanted a building that was easy to navigate, and in which it was easy to find people. Windows into labs and equipment rooms, a central atrium that acts as a ‘street’ (Figure 3), and breakout areas that are quiet (but visible) have enabled us to achieve this. The end result is a building carefully adapted to the culture of the LMB, with a particular emphasis on interaction and communal sharing. And although the new building is twice as large as the previous one, it feels more coherent.

![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/00856/elife-00856-fig3-v1.jpg)

**Figure 3.:** The central atrium of the new LMB building. There are three floors of labs and offices, with services such as air ducts being located between the floors. The two white structures to the left of the staircase each house a meeting room and an office.

Behind the scenes, we paid particular attention to the services in the building and their future flexibility. Unusually for a European building, there are full-height interstitial zones between the floors, which mean that the air ducts, pipework and wiring can all be accessed for maintenance and modification. Elsewhere, the main air handling units and other plant are not on the roof, as they usually are, but in towers adjacent to the building. This takes weight and vibration away from the lab structure and also creates iconic stainless steel-clad features to bemuse the onlooker.

## Challenges for the future

A pressing question in these hard economic times is whether the LMB style of science, with its need for relatively secure, long-term funding, will continue to be supported as governments seek quantifiable and preferably rapid returns on their investments in research. The latter approach tends to result in the avoidance of risk and the setting of defined targets, making it largely incompatible with difficult, long-term projects. Although grants can focus funding on particular projects, institutes that rely on grants for overheads cannot have the same level of flexibility and freedom, and may struggle when grants dry up.

At the LMB we would argue, as the evidence of the past supports, that core funding of long-term ambitious projects decided upon by scientists is still worthwhile. We also firmly believe that such funding will create an environment that is attractive to industry, will train the world's best scientists for the future, and will directly or indirectly generate discoveries, applications, medical advances and wealth. Some of the major research charities, notably the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the Wellcome Trust, recognize the need for longer term, more flexible funding and they have tailored their support accordingly, empowering the best scientists to be bold. The LMB has always done this.

The challenge for the LMB is to maintain scientific quality in the face of ever-increasing competition and, at the same time, to preserve a distinctive way of doing science. We now have an excellent building in which to operate, and every reason to work hard.

results.result: The LMB has a divisional organizational structure with four divisions (cell biology, neurobiology, protein and nucleic acid chemistry, and structural studies), where division heads and the director collectively make strategic decisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 provide straightforward factual descriptions of the LMB's organizational and governance structure. These are verifiable institutional facts presented explicitly in the text with no experimental or analytical components requiring validation.

results.result: Fred Sanger's strategic guidance led Greg Winter to apply protein engineering to antibodies rather than enzymes, resulting in the humanization of monoclonal antibodies—a breakthrough that revolutionized medicine and spawned three successful biotech companies.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7, C77-C78 form a coherent historical narrative about a strategic decision at the LMB. The facts about Sanger's position (C3), his suggestion (C4), Winter's achievement (C5), and the medical impact (C6-C7) are well-documented historical events that can be independently verified. This represents a concrete example of successful strategic guidance at the LMB.

results.result: The LMB pursues ambitious long-term research projects that can take over twenty years to complete, including ongoing analysis of the nematode nervous system and work on G-protein coupled receptor structures that originated from bacteriorhodopsin studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 describe the LMB's commitment to long-term research projects with specific examples. These are factual statements about ongoing research programs and their historical origins that are verifiable and consistent with the LMB's known research portfolio.

results.result: The LMB pioneered both X-ray crystallography and electron microscopy for protein structure determination and maintains a commitment to world-leading capabilities in determining large structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 describe well-documented historical contributions of the LMB to structural biology and its current strategic focus. These are verifiable facts about the institution's scientific legacy and stated priorities.

results.result: The LMB's operational philosophy holds that hiring the brightest scientists and allowing them autonomy to identify research opportunities, supported by central funding and flexibility, is the best approach to achieving breakthroughs, as major discoveries often come from unexpected directions.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 present the LMB's philosophical approach to research management. While C14 and C15 are marked as speculation and represent institutional beliefs rather than empirically tested hypotheses, the approach is supported by historical examples (like Winter's work). However, no comparative data or controlled assessment is provided to validate this as 'the best way' versus alternative approaches.

results.result: The LMB's recruitment strategy emphasizes building complementary research groups while prioritizing candidates who are bright, flexible, and imaginative over their specific research area, with most recruitment at the early career stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 describe the LMB's stated recruitment policies and priorities. These are institutional practices that are explicitly stated and represent the organization's approach to building its scientific workforce.

results.result: Venki Ramakrishnan, who shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for ribosome structure work, moved from the US to the LMB because it offered the long-term support and security needed for such an ambitious project.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 present verifiable historical facts about Ramakrishnan's Nobel Prize and career move, along with his stated motivation. The Nobel Prize is a matter of public record, and the motivation is presented as Ramakrishnan's own assessment.

results.result: At the LMB, peer pressure provides the primary motivation for excellent work, facilitated by encouraged interactions where informal conversations and seminar feedback can be as influential as formal directives.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 describe the LMB's cultural approach to motivation and scientific exchange. These are institutional practices and cultural observations that are consistently stated and align with the overall description of the LMB's collaborative environment.

results.result: The LMB strategically maintains proximity to Addenbrooke's Hospital and industry contacts, is integrating part of Cambridge University's Department of Medicine into its new building, and has dedicated space for translational projects, with successful collaborations arising from voluntary partnerships rather than compulsion.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 describe the LMB's physical location, institutional relationships, and collaborative philosophy. These are verifiable facts about location, building plans, and stated institutional experience with collaboration approaches.

results.result: The new LMB building design retained key features from the old building (workshops, rooftop restaurant) while expanding specialist equipment space and improving maintainability, using a scientist-centered design approach that started with bench layouts.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C37 describe the design goals and approach for the new building. While C37 includes subjective language ('undoubtedly the best way'), the overall description of design priorities and methodology is presented as factual institutional decision-making.

results.result: The new building's layout promotes the LMB's hands-on culture and interaction through write-up spaces near benches, intermingled group leader offices, partially divided labs, accessible equipment rooms across corridors, and maintained scientist density matching the original building—all designed to encourage the researcher interactions that characterized the original LMB.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C43, C75-C76 describe specific architectural features and their intended purposes. These are factual descriptions of the building layout supported by the provided figures, with explicit design intentions stated by the institution. The connection to the original building's characteristics (C76) provides historical context.

results.result: The new LMB building incorporates windows into labs and equipment rooms, a central atrium functioning as a 'street,' and quiet but visible breakout areas to facilitate navigation and finding people, resulting in a building twice the size of its predecessor that feels more coherent and emphasizes interaction and communal sharing.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 describe architectural features and their functional purposes, supported by Figure 3. While C49 includes a subjective assessment ('feels more coherent'), the overall description of features and design philosophy is factual and verifiable from the building itself.

results.result: The new building incorporates unusual (for Europe) full-height interstitial zones between floors for accessible maintenance of building services, with main air handling units located in adjacent towers rather than on the roof to reduce weight and vibration on lab structures while creating distinctive architectural features.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C57 describe specific engineering and architectural features of the building. These are factual descriptions of building systems and their functional benefits, supported by Figure 3. The claim about these features being unusual for European buildings (C51) represents stated institutional knowledge.

results.result: The sustainability of the LMB's long-term funding model is questioned in the current economic climate where governments increasingly seek rapid, quantifiable returns on research investment—an approach that tends toward risk avoidance and defined targets, making it incompatible with difficult long-term projects.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 present a coherent argument about funding pressures and their implications. While these involve some inference (C60-C61), they represent reasonable observations about research funding trends and their logical consequences for long-term research programs.

results.result: Institutes relying on grants for overhead costs cannot achieve the same flexibility and freedom as the LMB and face vulnerability when grant funding decreases.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 present logical inferences about the constraints of grant-dependent funding models. These are reasonable institutional observations about the structural differences between funding approaches and their implications for operational flexibility.

results.result: The LMB argues that historical evidence supports the value of core funding for long-term scientist-directed projects, believing such funding creates environments attractive to industry, trains top scientists, and generates discoveries, applications, medical advances, and wealth.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 references historical evidence but doesn't provide specific data or analysis. Claims C65-C67 are explicitly marked as speculation and represent institutional beliefs about future outcomes rather than demonstrated results. While the LMB's historical success provides some support, the causal claims about core funding's effects lack rigorous comparative evidence.

results.result: Major research charities including the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Wellcome Trust have recognized the need for and implemented longer-term, more flexible funding to empower bold scientific work—an approach the LMB has historically practiced.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 describe the funding philosophies of major research organizations and the LMB's historical approach. These are verifiable facts about institutional funding policies and the LMB's stated historical practices.

results.result: The LMB faces the dual challenge of maintaining scientific quality amid increasing competition while preserving its distinctive approach to science, now operating from an excellent new building.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 present the institution's stated challenges and current status. These are straightforward statements about institutional goals and the completion of the new building facility.
